in_context.text: Paul tells Timothy to honour "widows indeed," meaning widows with no one else (5:3, 5:5). This verse sets out the other case. If a widow has children or grandchildren, they should care for her first, and the church should not carry that load (5:16).

speaker.text: Paul the apostle, writing to Timothy. The letter names Paul as author (1:1), though many scholars think a follower wrote in his name.

audience.text: Timothy, whom Paul left to lead the church at Ephesus. Timothy is to pass these instructions on to the church (5:7).

affected.text: The children and grandchildren of widows, who are told to care for them. The widows themselves are also affected, since they are the ones being cared for.

what.text: Family members should learn to put their faith into practice at home first. They do this by repaying what they owe to the parents and grandparents who raised them. Paul says God approves of this.

events.text: The verse is an instruction, not a story, so it describes no particular event. It addresses an ongoing need in the church at Ephesus.

written.text: Traditional view: about AD 62-64, between Paul's two Roman imprisonments. Scholarly view: many critical scholars date it around AD 80-110 and see it as written by a follower of Paul, while others defend the earlier date.

where.text: The instructions were for the church in Ephesus, a wealthy port city and capital of the Roman province of Asia. The letter does not say where it was written from, though Paul may have been in Macedonia.

purpose.text: The church had limited means to support widows. Paul wants families to support their own widows, so the church can help those who truly have no one (5:16). Failing to provide for one's own household is called a denial of the faith (5:8).

big_picture.text: This verse belongs to a section on caring for groups in the church, such as widows, elders, and servants. It reflects a key theme of the letter: belief and behaviour belong together. It echoes the command "Honour thy father and mother" (Matthew 15:4).

for_readers.text: Faith is shown first in how we treat our own families, especially aging parents. Jesus did the same when he gave his mother into the care of the beloved disciple from the cross (John 19:26-27).

why_it_matters.text: In older English, "nephews" here translates a Greek word meaning descendants, that is, grandchildren. The verse is about a widow's own children and grandchildren, not her siblings' sons.
This verb means to show reverence or devotion. It is used elsewhere for worshipping God (Acts 17:23). Here it is aimed at one's own household, which treats family care as a real act of devotion.
The word means repayment or recompense. Paired with a verb for paying what is due, it frames caring for parents as returning a debt, not as optional charity.
This word usually means forebears or ancestors. Here it refers to living parents and grandparents, the older generation who raised the family.
This is the same word Paul uses in 2:3 for what pleases God. It puts caring for family alongside prayer as something God welcomes.

takeaway.text: Caring for your own aging parents and grandparents is a basic part of faith, and God approves of it. Families should carry this duty first, so the church can help those who have no one.

unsupported.reason: The lexicon only says the word means 'acceptable' and also appears in 1 Timothy 2:3. It says nothing about the context of 2:3, so linking family care with prayer goes beyond the cited source.
